messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas, a 56‑year‑old guitarist from a small Midwestern town, recalls the night he was assaulted in a dim, abandoned warehouse on a late spring evening. He was alone, rehearsing a new set when a man he’d met online slipped his hand under the curtain. The man’s sudden violence, the splash of blood, and the scent of a floral perfume he wore left Thomas in a stunned, terrified haze. From that moment on, each flash of bright light, each whiff of cologne, and each glimpse of blood has become a trigger that instantly reminds him of that assault, pushing him into a state of heightened threat. The flashbacks are not seamless. Thomas reports that his memory of the assault is blocked before it can fully form; some moments of the night are starkly vivid, others are blank. The incomplete, fragmented recollection fuels his belief that he can’t reconstruct the story, so he pushes the memory away. That avoidance keeps the traumatic episode alive in his mind as an unresolved threat, and when a trigger—a stain of blood on a stage curtain, a bottle of perfume on a backstage table—arises, the memory surges again, and his sense of danger spikes. The threat he feels is not only the possibility of a new assault; it is also the feeling that every sudden movement by someone around him could be a danger, and he has learned to see the world through that lens. Because the threat is so pervasive, Thomas has developed a set of maladaptive strategies that keep him safe, in his own sense. He refuses to express anger at all, believing that showing any emotion would invite the same violence he feared. He avoids any authority figure—a stage manager, a band leader, even a receptionist at the music store—because their presence feels like an escalation of power that could threaten him. He also steers clear of social contacts, particularly former bandmates and friends who were there before the assault, fearing that their memories might echo the violence he endured. Suppressing anger, avoiding authority, and shunning social contacts keep the memory from being fully processed; the memory stays unintegrated, and the threat never recedes. The constant threat heightens his sensitivity to triggers: a sudden movement on stage or the scent of perfume can suddenly make his heart pound and his hands tremble. In turn, these triggers reawaken the incomplete memory, which again fuels his avoidance and threat, creating a tightening loop. In the studio, Thomas’s avoidance has tangible effects. He rarely performs with his band, preferring to stay in the rehearsal space alone. When a new guitarist joins, Thomas’s fear of authority figures turns the session into a tense, awkward affair. His wife, Maria, has noticed how he withdraws from rehearsal, how he refuses to practice with the band because of the sudden movement of people around him. The couple’s communication has frayed; Maria has taken on more responsibilities at home because Thomas cannot attend community concerts or share his music with friends. The occupational demands of being a musician—rehearsing, performing, traveling—now feel like constant threats that push him into isolation. The accumulation of these patterns finally brought Thomas to the clinic. After a particularly jarring rehearsal where a microphone cable flickered and a backstage door slammed, he realized that his avoidance had left him alone with his memories and his sense of danger, unable to share even a small piece of his experience. He feared that if he continued to suppress his anger and avoid people, his life would become a series of empty rooms and silent concerts. He hopes that therapy can help him dismantle the loop that keeps his memory trapped, his triggers relentless, and his threat ever-present, and that he can finally feel safe enough to express himself, both in music and in conversation.
